items.text: I found a useful bound while preserving the run’s state. With the rim fixed, those three northern cells can contain at most 1, 6, and 92 pickups. Even distributing every other pickup optimally among the remaining cells gives variance at least **1,467**, above K-means’ **1,374**. That bound follows from their fixed edges and convexity; annealing cannot remove it. Moving the rim is therefore a necessary test.

The 90-round map is being reproduced and saved as an exact vertex configuration, so the next strategy starts from it rather than rebuilding a fresh grid. I’ve also corrected the temperature definition: for 5,986 pickups and 38 cells, it is exactly zero when every affected cell has **157 or 158** pickups.

Starting from the saved 90-round map worked. With rim vertices allowed to participate, variance fell from **4,200 to 3,694 in ten more rounds**. The test retains convexity, the shape threshold, all pickups, and 234 sampled land or shoreline points that the starting map covered. I’m continuing and will inspect whether any coverage is lost between those samples.

The warm-started movable-rim run is at **3,263 variance after 30 rounds**. That confirms the fixed rim was a real obstacle, although the result is still far from balanced. I’m preserving each best state and will check the final map for shape and geographic coverage, since the coverage test is currently sampled.

Yes, Udi. I tested the restrictions on the same 5,986 pickups and 38 cells.

| Trial | Final population variance | What happened |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Current rule: convex, shape score ≥ 0.35 | 6,250 | Stalled |
| Remove the shape bound; keep convexity | 6,578 | No improvement |
| Also search farther for each vertex | 6,717 | No improvement |
| Allow nonconvex cells | 4,185 | Better balance, but 30 cells became nonconvex and the worst shape score fell to 0.069 |

I also tested your suggestion in a limited form: moving a vertex and its adjacent vertices together, with each neighbour following 55% of its displacement. It stayed convex but stalled at **6,976**. That tests one coordinated motion, not your broader idea.

The promising relaxation is **independent, atomic movement of nearby vertices**. The active vertex would propose positions for itself and selected neighbours; we would check convexity and pickup counts in *every cell touched by the group*, then commit the whole move only if total imbalance falls. Intermediate positions need not be valid because they are never committed. That preserves your local agent rule while giving it substantially more freedom than moving one corner at a time.
I should have generated the comparison before stopping. I’m producing a new side-by-side figure from the same pickup data and 38-region setting, with the revised hexagon result on the right.

items.text: I found the main failure: the current force points a corner according to population differences, but it never checks whether the move actually improves those differences. I’m replacing that with a local trial rule that counts pickups in the three affected cells before accepting a move, while enforcing convexity and a shape bound.

This folder holds one interactive web page: Manhattan_Taxi_Regions.html
It runs entirely in your web browser. Nothing to install, no internet needed

HOW TO OPEN

WHAT YOU WILL SEE

24,101 real yellow-taxi pickups in Manhattan (15 January 2015, 8-9 am),

  Hexagon               A honeycomb of K hexagons whose corners move toward

Use the sliders on the right to change the parameters; Play / Run starts

A honeycomb of K hexagons covers Manhattan (only hexagons that touch the island are kept), and its corners are the agents. items.text:
Udi, I implemented the local rule in the simulator: each vertex tests positions using only its three adjacent hexagons and moves only when their pickup imbalance decreases. Accepted moves must keep those hexagons convex and above a shape bound.

In a 20-round check with 38 hexagons, squared pickup imbalance fell from **2,799,304 to 1,226,528** without increasing in any round. This is a local improvement rule, so it may still settle before all populations are equal.

[Download the revised simulator](sandbox:/workspace/scratch/289abe85887d/Manhattan_Taxi_Regions_Local_Rule.zip)

No, Udi. I overstated what those two changes would accomplish.

The **convexity check** would prevent inward folds, but a convex hexagon can still be extremely long and thin. Activating each vertex once per round would make the scheduling more even; it would not ensure that the cell populations equalize. The implementation already preserves six vertices per cell.

So those are useful corrections, but **they do not fix the result in the screenshot**. We need to examine the vertex movement rule and its objective before claiming the simulation implements the density equalization we specified.
